entities.summary:
Jean Rolin (1408–1483), a prominent French prelate, rose to the cardinalate and served as a pivotal figure in the political and ecclesiastical landscape of 15th-century Western Europe, particularly within the orbit of the powerful Duchy of Burgundy. Born into a distinguished Burgundian noble family, his career was marked by a skillful navigation of complex diplomatic and theological currents, notably during the Great Western Schism and the conciliar movement. As a trusted advisor to Duke Philip the Good, Rolin wielded significant influence, embodying the close intertwining of secular power and ecclesiastical authority characteristic of the late medieval period.

Rolin's ascent began with his appointment as Bishop of Autun in 1431, a crucial see within the Duchy. His diplomatic acumen quickly became apparent as he represented Burgundy at the Council of Basel from 1432, advocating for conciliar supremacy over papal authority in its early phases. A crowning achievement of his diplomatic efforts was his instrumental role in negotiating the Treaty of Arras in 1435, which reconciled Philip the Good with King Charles VII of France, thereby extricating Burgundy from its alliance with England and fundamentally altering the course of the Hundred Years' War. Despite his earlier conciliar leanings, Rolin ultimately reconciled with Pope Eugene IV, who elevated him to cardinal in 1448, recognizing his strategic importance and influence within the Burgundian court.
